lesson.menu_desc: Phase 4 -- when the trip goes wrong, explain why and what it led to, with cause and result clauses -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 33 -- Because of the Rain... -- Cause and Result
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 33 -- Because of the Rain...
lesson.grammar_point: cause and result clauses (because of, due to and owing to + noun, because, since and as + clause, so + adjective + that, such + noun + that, which is why, and lead to / result in)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you told other people what to do. Today something goes wrong, and you explain why. Travel is where English needs cause and result the most, because nothing ever goes exactly to plan. Start with the cause. English has two families here, and mixing them is the most common mistake at this level. Because of, due to and owing to are followed by a noun. Because of the rain. Due to the typhoon. Because, since and as are followed by a full sentence, with a subject and a verb. Because it was raining. Since the trains had stopped. So never say because of it was raining. That is the first trap. Now the result. The simplest word is so. It rained all day, so we stayed in. Then there are two patterns that measure how big the cause was. So, plus an adjective, plus that. The delay was so long that we missed the connection. Such, plus a noun, plus that. It was such a long delay that we missed the connection. So goes with the adjective alone, and such goes with a noun. Never so a long delay. That is the second trap. The third trap looks innocent. So that is not a result. So that means in order to. I left early so that I would not miss the train. That is a purpose. It rained, so that we stayed in, is wrong. Two more links make you sound like a real storyteller. Which is why, after a comma, turns the whole first sentence into a cause. The flight was overbooked, which is why we got a voucher. And lead to, or result in, when one thing produces another. The storm led to three hundred cancellations. Before class, think of a day when one small thing went wrong and caused everything else, and tell it to yourself one link at a time. See you in class, Mark.

Good afternoon. This is an announcement for all passengers departing from Terminal Three this afternoon. Due to a typhoon warning for the Tokyo area, all departures scheduled after two p.m. have been grounded. We know this is not the news you wanted. Because the wind is expected to get stronger in the next few hours, no flights will leave the airport before tomorrow morning at the earliest. As a result, every afternoon flight has been cancelled, and the airlines are rebooking passengers on the first available departures. Please do not go to your gate. Go to your airline's service desk on the departures level, where the staff will rebook you. If your new flight leaves tomorrow, you are entitled to a hotel voucher, which is why we ask you to keep your boarding pass with you. The trains to the city are still running, but they are extremely crowded, owing to the number of passengers leaving the airport at the same time. If you do not need to travel into the city tonight, we recommend that you stay in the terminal, where food and water will be available all night. The next announcement will be at four o'clock. Thank you for your patience.

extra_audio.text: It started on Friday morning, when a typhoon warning was announced for Tokyo. Because of the wind, every afternoon flight was grounded, and nobody could leave. As a result, we were stranded at the airport with about a thousand other people. The airline rebooked us for Sunday, which is why we got a hotel voucher for two nights. In the end we made the best of it, and we spent a free Saturday walking around the city in the rain.
